HW 13: Your first Stan programs

Due: Thursday, Apr 29 at 2:30 pm on Canvas · Size: full analysis · Points: 25 · Covers: Stan basics and IRT

Start from the homework template, use ## Q1 to ## Q5 headings, and turn in both the .qmd and the rendered .html.

The big idea. All semester, brms has been writing Stan programs for you (you may have peeked in the “Under the hood” boxes). Now you’ll write two yourself: first a model you already know, so you can check you got it right, then a 2PL IRT model, the kind of model where writing Stan directly is often easier than coaxing brms into it.

Setup. You already have Stan installed through {cmdstanr}. In R, a Stan program can live in a string; write_stan_file() saves it and cmdstan_model() compiles it:

library(cmdstanr)
library(posterior)
library(tidybayes)

code <- "
data { ... }
parameters { ... }
model { ... }
"
mod <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(code))
fit <- mod$sample(data = list(...), seed = 13, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4)
fit$summary()
draws <- as_draws_df(fit$draws())      # works with tidybayes / ggplot like any other draws

Stan is picky: every statement ends in ;, every variable has a declared type, and comments start with //. When it won’t compile, read the error message’s line number first.

Part A: a model you already know (Q1–Q2)

Use your HW 2 data and priors (your own data, or sat.act: SATV predicted by centered ACT).

Q1. Write the regression in Stan (5 points)

  1. Fill in the TODOs in this skeleton with your HW 2 model (likelihood and the three priors):
data {
  int<lower=1> N;        // number of people
  vector[N] x;           // predictor (centered)
  vector[N] y;           // outcome
}
parameters {
  real alpha;            // intercept
  real beta;             // slope
  real<lower=0> sigma;   // residual SD (the <lower=0> matters: why?)
}
model {
  // priors
  alpha ~ TODO;
  beta  ~ TODO;
  sigma ~ TODO;
  // likelihood
  y ~ TODO;
}
  1. Fit it with cmdstanr. Check R-hat and ESS in fit$summary().
  2. Compare the posterior for the intercept, slope, and σ with your HW 2 brms fit (a small table is enough). They should match to within Monte Carlo error. Do they? If not, what’s different? (Hint: compare with stancode() of your brms model. Did brms center anything, or put the prior on a different intercept?)
  3. Why does sigma need <lower=0>? What would go wrong without it?

Q2. Make Stan compute something for you (5 points)

Add a generated quantities block that computes, for every posterior draw:

  • mu_new: the expected outcome for a person with a predictor value you choose (pass it in as data, e.g., real x_new;);
  • y_new: a predicted outcome for one new person at that value (normal_rng());
  • y_rep: a full replicated dataset (vector[N] y_rep; filled in a loop with normal_rng()).

Then: report mu_new and y_new with 95% intervals (why is one wider?), and use y_rep to make your own posterior predictive check (e.g., bayesplot::ppc_dens_overlay(y, yrep_matrix)). In two or three sentences: what does generated quantities let you do that would be awkward otherwise?

Part B: a 2PL IRT model (Q3–Q5)

The LSAT data: 1,000 people answered 5 law-school-admission items, each scored correct (1) or incorrect (0). This is a classic IRT dataset. Put it in long format, one row per person × item:

lsat <- read_csv("https://bayes27.netlify.app/LSAT.csv") |>
  mutate(person = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("item"), names_to = "item", values_to = "y") |>
  mutate(item = as.integer(str_remove(item, "item")))

The two-parameter logistic (2PL) model says the probability that person p gets item i right depends on the person’s ability θp, the item’s difficulty bi, and its discrimination ai:

\[ \begin{aligned} y_{pi} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_{pi}) \\ \text{logit}(\pi_{pi}) &= a_i(\theta_p - b_i) \\ \theta_p &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1) \\ b_i &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 2) \\ a_i &\sim \text{LogNormal}(0, 0.5) \end{aligned} \]

Q3. Write and fit the 2PL (5 points)

  1. Fill in the TODOs:
data {
  int<lower=1> N;                        // number of responses (people x items)
  int<lower=1> P;                        // number of people
  int<lower=1> I;                        // number of items
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=P> person; // which person gave response n
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=I> item;   // which item response n is for
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> y;      // correct (1) or not (0)
}
parameters {
  vector[P] theta;                       // person ability
  vector[I] b;                           // item difficulty
  vector<lower=0>[I] a;                  // item discrimination
}
model {
  theta ~ TODO;
  b ~ TODO;
  a ~ TODO;
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(TODO);             // hint: a[item] .* (theta[person] - b[item])
}
  1. Fit it and check the diagnostics. How many parameters did you just estimate? Compare that with the number of data points.
  2. Two things make this model identified: θ ~ Normal(0, 1) and a constrained to be positive. In your own words, what would go wrong without each one? (Hint: if you added 1 to every θ and every b, would the likelihood change? What if you flipped the sign of every θ and every a?)

Q4. What do the items tell you? (5 points)

  1. Report each item’s difficulty and discrimination with 95% intervals. Which item is hardest? Which best separates high- from low-ability people?
  2. Check your answers against a maximum-likelihood 2PL from {ltm}: ltm::ltm(LSAT ~ z1, IRT.param = TRUE) (use the wide data with only the item columns). Do they agree? Why might the Bayesian estimates be a bit different for the easiest items?
  3. Look back at the lecture’s brms version of the 2PL (non-linear syntax with exp(logalpha) * delta). In two or three sentences: which version is easier to read and why? What would you need to change in your Stan code to turn this into a 1PL (Rasch) model?

Q5. Publication-ready item characteristic curves (5 points)

Make a figure that meets the checklist showing the item characteristic curves (probability of a correct answer across ability, θ from −4 to 3) for all five items, computed from your posterior draws (π = logistic(a(θ − b)), draw by draw), with 95% ribbons.

  • Label items clearly, use a colorblind-safe palette with a second cue, and label the x-axis in words (e.g., “Ability (θ, SD units)”).
  • Write a stand-alone caption, use ggsave() at 6.5 inches wide, and write one or two sentences on what the figure says about this test (hint: who is it good at measuring?).
Going further: from 2PL to a drift diffusion model (optional, not graded)

The same workflow scales to cognitive models. A drift diffusion model describes a speeded two-choice decision as evidence accumulating toward one of two boundaries; it predicts response times and choices together. Stan has it built in as wiener_lpdf(), and brms wraps it as family = wiener(). The Stan model has exactly the same structure as your 2PL: data, parameters (drift rate, boundary separation, non-decision time, bias), priors, and one likelihood line. If you’re headed toward cognitive modeling, try writing one for a simulated dataset (RWiener::rwiener() simulates data).
